g_rules.text: Newsletter output has chosen subject line plus 2 alternatives
Output includes preview text
Full issue in markdown, formatted for email readability
Output includes image suggestions with placement notes
Notes teaser is 2-3 sentences
Ghostwriting: output includes the voice guide used

Voice guide follows template: name, Created, Sources used, Core (register, sentence length, humor, confidence), Vocabulary (uses, avoids, technical level), Structural patterns (opens, closes, paragraphs, lists/prose), Signature moves, Things that would sound wrong
Anti-pattern lines read '[anti-pattern]: would sound like [wrong voice] instead of [right voice]'
Signature moves each give a specific pattern with an example from source material
Voice guide holds 10-15 markers with examples
Write in the client's voice, not your own; use the voice guide as a per-paragraph checklist
Do not over-polish; if the client speaks in fragments, keep fragments
Voice is defined by absence: never add things the client never uses (e.g. exclamation marks)
Do not make the client sound more formal or professional than they are
Subject line: specificity beats vagueness
Subject line promises a clear benefit or reveal
Subject line 6-10 words
If dev audience: technical keywords, 'How to' and numbers, no urgency or scarcity tactics
Front-load the interesting part of the subject (~35-40 chars visible on mobile, under 60 chars)
Preview text complements, does not repeat, the subject line
Preview text is about 90 characters, acting as the subhead
Subtitle (email preview line) under 10 words
Hook is 2-3 opening sentences built on a named strategy (credibility, counter-narrative, curiosity, surprise, data) and hooks within the first 2 sentences
After the hook, a 1-2 paragraph context: why this matters now, what prompted it
Body structure depends on content type
Takeaway of 1-2 sentences: the one thing to remember
CTA of 1-2 sentences asking a specific action; reply-inviting question preferred
End with a genuine question that invites replies
Share prompt: forward it to a colleague who [specific situation]
If recommendation partnerships exist, weave in natural cross-references
Notes teaser stands alone as valuable, not just a link
Email paragraphs 2-3 sentences max
Code in email: inline under 5 lines, fenced 5-10 with language hint, over 10 link to Gist with excerpt; backticks for identifiers
TL;DR at top for issues over 1500 words
Subheadings every 200-400 words (email: 300-400)
H2 for major sections, H3 for subsections, never deeper than H3
Bold the key phrase of each section so skimmers get the argument; 1-2 per section, do not over-bold
Descriptive link anchor text, never 'click here'; no URL shorteners
Place important links early in the issue
Lists sparingly: numbered for steps, bullets for comparisons or roundups; never for every section or for flowing prose
Horizontal rules only for major topic shifts, max 2-3 per issue
Blockquotes for quotes, a key insight, or a TL;DR
Never put critical information only in an image or embed
Images sparingly: 1-3 suggestions, a strong cover image first, at most 1-2 inline
Each image suggestion gives Placement, Purpose, Description
Always include alt text for images
Images break up text every 500-800 words
Diagrams and charts add value for technical content
Button text 3-5 words; max 1-2 buttons per issue
Suggest special blocks: subscribe button after the hook, share button after the strongest insight
Poll block: suggest for engagement, max one per post
Footnotes sparingly in email
Keep body under ~3000 words (Gmail clips at 102KB)
Length set by tier: Short 500-800, Standard 1000-1500, Deep dive 2000+
Humanize: strip filler words, predictable cadence, over-hedging, hollow transitions, inflated language
Ghostwriting captures the client's existing insights, not invented ones
Audience shapes register and depth (junior devs vs CTOs)
Objective shapes the CTA, hook angle, and where depth or link sits
If adapting existing content: cut 30-50% for newsletter, add personal layer, front-load value, add CTA

r_rules.text: Build voice guide first; from transcripts if given, else infer from briefs and say so in Sources used
Refresh rules for an existing guide (keep Core, refresh Signature moves)
Package parts in fixed order: subject, alternatives, preview, issue, images, Notes teaser, voice guide
==== banner strings and two blank lines before each
[Subscribe button] after intro, [Share button] near end
1: one chosen subject plus exactly two alternatives covering different angles
2: subject plain, specific, 5-10 words, no question marks or colons
3: preview 1-3 sentences, 10-18 words, names what the subject does not
4: H1 repeats subject verbatim, italic preview line under it
5: intro 2-4 short paragraphs, 60-110 words, one bolded key fact
6: first sentence a specific moment, number, or flat claim; opener by brief type
7: 3-7 H2 sections, short sentence-case, no puns
8: section order follows brief type
9: downside gets own first-person section
10: bold one key line per section, 5-12 total
11: numbered lists for steps, bullets for examples, 3-5 items
12: end matter order; one-sentence takeaway 'The thing to remember:'
13: optional Try it yourself section for rerunnable experiments
14: Your turn: one question, hit reply, small promise
15: forward line to a specific colleague
16: sign off with first name
17: issue 550-700 words
18: first person I/we, address reader as you 10-30 times, active voice for mistakes
19: short sentences and fragments, paragraphs 1-3 sentences
20: use contractions
21a: no emojis, hashtags, exclamation marks
21b: no em dashes, en dashes, double hyphens
22: numbers before lesson, plain verbs, metaphors from author's field
23: no inspirational framing or hype
24: two images (cover + inline tied to H2), Placement/Purpose/Description/Alt text
25: flat descriptions, chart or diagram for data, no strangers' faces
26: Notes teaser one standalone first-person paragraph, 35-55 words
27: voice guide fixed headings and bullet counts, anti-pattern 'would sound like X instead of Y'
28: issue obeys the guide's hard limits

lessons: Platform mechanics rules (code-block limits, link placement, anchor text, TL;DR thresholds, button word counts) never fire on short non-technical samples. Ask the user directly which conditional formatting rules exist for content types not in the sample.

Length tiers hide behind a single observed range. When every output lands in one band, ask whether that band is one choice among several (short, standard, deep) rather than encoding it as the fixed rule.

Voice-fidelity rules (do not over-polish, do not formalize, respect what the author never does) shape ghostwritten output but leave no trace when the author is invented. Ask how voice is protected, not only what the voice guide looks like.

Structural numbers stated as caps (paragraph max 3 sentences, max 2-3 dividers, 1-2 bold per section, 10-15 voice markers) get recovered as observed ranges that can exceed the cap. Check whether an observed range should be stated as a hard ceiling.
